Theme

wake someone up verb

also wake, waken, awaken, rouse

classical

Suet. Calig. 6 (Lewis & Short)

expergēfaciō, expergēfacere, expergēfēcī, expergēfactum

verb, third conjugation

Lewis & Short cite it of waking from sleep only from Suetonius and the Vulgate; Cicero and Livy say excitō.

Other words

  • excitō, excitāre, excitāvī, excitātum — wake, rouse (from sleep)

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Liv. 5.47.3: nē canēs quidem … excitārent; Cic. Rep. 6.12: nē mē ē somnō excitētis (Lewis & Short); Traupman 39, 403: wake up, tr., (ē somnō) excitāre

    The usual verb of classical prose, often with ē somnō.

  • suscitō, suscitāre, suscitāvī, suscitātum — wake, rouse

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Most. 372c: Suscitā istum, Delphium.; Cic. Tusc. 4.44: aliquem ē somnō (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • Suscitā istum, Delphium. — Callidamatēs, Callidamatēs, vigilā.

    Wake him up, Delphium. — Callidamates, Callidamates, wake up!Plaut. Most. 372c–373

  • tantō silentiō in summum ēvāsēre ut nōn custōdēs sōlum fallerent, sed nē canēs quidem, sollicitum animal ad nocturnōs strepitūs, excitārent

    they reached the top so quietly that they slipped past the guards and did not even wake the dogs, creatures that fret at every noise in the nightLiv. 5.47.3

  • hī nostrī vigilēs nocturnī, quōs excitandīs in opera mortālibus rumpendōque somnō nātūra genuit

    these night watchmen of ours, whom nature made to wake us mortals for our work and break our sleepPlin. NH 10.46

See also wake up.
